“Personally Identifiable Information”

Personally Identifiable Information collected by Sunstate Family Practice is securely stored and is not accessible to third parties or employees of Sunstate Family Practice except for use as indicated above.

Visitors and Authorized Customers may opt out of receiving unsolicited information from or being contacted by us and/or our vendors and affiliated agencies by responding to emails as instructed, or by contacting us at 3207 7744.
Are Cookies Used on the Site?

Cookies are used for a variety of reasons. We use Cookies to obtain information about the preferences of our Visitors and the services they select. We also use Cookies for security purposes to protect our Authorized Customers. For example, if an Authorized Customer is logged on and the site is unused for more than 10 minutes, we may automatically log the Authorized Customer off.

While we take commercially reasonable measures to maintain a secure site, electronic communications and databases are subject to errors, tampering and break-ins, and we cannot guarantee or warrant that such events will not take place and we will not be liable to Visitors or Authorized Customers for any such occurrences.

What happens if the Privacy Policy Changes?

We will let our Visitors and Authorized Customers know about changes to our privacy policy by posting such changes on the Site. title: Skin Checks Redland Bay - GP Skin Cancer Checks | Sunstate Family Practice
description: Looking for skin checks near Redland Bay? Our experienced GPs provide comprehensive skin examinations, mole assessments and ongoing skin monitoring.

blocks.html: Living in South East Queensland means spending plenty of time outdoors. While enjoying the sunshine is part of our lifestyle, regular exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation can increase the risk of skin cancer over time. Queensland has one of the highest rates of skin cancer in the world, making routine skin checks an important part of preventive healthcare.
If you live in Redland Bay, our experienced GPs provide comprehensive skin checks for patients who want to monitor their skin health or have concerns about new or changing spots.
Whether you’re due for a routine skin examination or you’ve noticed a mole or lesion that looks different, we’re here to help assess your skin and discuss the most appropriate next steps.

What Is a Skin Check?​

A skin check is a thorough examination of your skin performed by a GP inRedland Bay. During the appointment, your doctor will assess moles, freckles and other skin lesions across your body, looking for features that may require monitoring or further investigation.

If an area of concern is identified, your GP will explain their findings and discuss appropriate management options, which may include monitoring, biopsy, treatment or referral where clinically indicated.
Not every unusual spot is skin cancer, but having changes assessed promptly is important.

blocks.text: Who Should Have Regular Skin Checks?
blocks.html: Who Should Have Regular Skin Checks?
Skin checks may be appropriate for adults of all ages, particularly those who have one or more risk factors, including the following:

items: Fair skin that burns easily
A history of significant sun exposure or sunburn
Outdoor work or recreational activities
A large number of moles
Previous skin cancer
A family history of melanoma or other skin cancers
A weakened immune system

blocks.html: If you’re unsure how often you should have your skin checked, your GP from Redland Bay can provide personalised advice based on your individual risk factors.

blocks.text: Signs You Should Book a Skin Check
blocks.html: Signs You Should Book a Skin Check
Arrange an appointment if you notice:

items: A new mole or skin spot
A mole that has changed in size, shape or colour
A lesion that bleeds or crusts
A sore that doesn’t heal
A spot that itches, becomes tender or painful
Any skin change that concerns you

blocks.html: If you’re worried about any change to your skin, it’s important to seek medical assessment rather than attempting to diagnose it yourself.

blocks.text: How to prepare for your appointment
blocks.html: How to prepare for your appointment
A few simple steps can make your skin check smoother:

items: Wear comfortable clothing that is easy to remove
Avoid heavy makeup or thick fake tan on the day
Remove nail polish if you have any spots on your fingers or toes that you are worried about
Bring a list of any previous skin cancers or biopsies, if you have it

blocks.html: If you are uncomfortable with a full body examination, let yourRedland Bay GP know. You can agree together which areas will be checked.

blocks.text: What Happens During Your Appointment in Redland Bay?
blocks.html: What Happens During Your Appointment in Redland Bay?
Your in Redland Bay GP will:

items: Discuss your medical and skin history
Ask about any new or changing spots you’ve noticed.
Examine your skin, including areas that are difficult for you to see yourself
Use dermoscopy where appropriate to assist with the assessment of skin lesions
Explain any findings and recommend suitable follow-up if required

blocks.html: The appointment is designed to be thorough while allowing time to answer any questions you may have.
Skin Monitoring Technology
Where clinically appropriate, our clinic uses high-quality imaging and dermoscopy to assist with the assessment and documentation of skin lesions.

For some patients, photographic documentation may help monitor changes in selected lesions over time as part of an ongoing skin surveillance plan. The suitability of this approach depends on your individual circumstances and will be discussed during your consultation.
Why Regular Skin Checks Matter
Many skin cancers can develop without causing pain or other symptoms in their early stages. Regular skin examinations can help identify suspicious lesions that may require further investigation.
Redland Bay GP will recommend an appropriate review schedule based on your personal risk profile, previous history and examination findings.

items: Full skin examinations

blocks.q: Do your doctors perform Telephone Consultations?

a.html: Yes. We charge a fee for Telehealth consultations (Medicare rebate currently applies provided you have been seen in person by a doctor at our practice in the past 12 months). Please book via our website or HotDoc app.

blocks.q: How do you protect my privacy?

a.html: We value your privacy and rights and have safeguards to ensure that your medical record is only accessible to authorised staff. We abide by the 13 Australian National Privacy Principles. A copy of our privacy policy is available at reception andhere. The National Privacy Commissioner is able to receive complaints concerning privacy issues on 1300 363 992 or oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-complaints.

blocks.q: How do I receive my results?

blocks.q: Can I request a script or referral without a consultation?

blocks.q: Am I able to see a doctor of my choice?

For unwell matters, please phone the surgery to be triaged on the day if there is no appointment availability online. On occasions, your usual doctor may be unavailable, and depending on the urgency of the matter, you may be offered an appointment with an alternative doctor.

blocks.html: Skin Cancer Checks
At Sunstate Family Practice

Queensland has some of the highest rates of skin cancer in the world, so regular skin checks are not a luxury. They are part of looking after your health, just like a blood pressure or cholesterol check.

At Sunstate Family Practice in Victoria Point, the GPs offer thorough skin checks that fit within your broader health care. We look after your moles and your general health at the same visit, which makes life simpler.
If you cannot remember your last skin check, that is usually a sign it has been too long.
Introducing our new service​
Total Body Mapping (TBM)​
Track your skin’s story with precision. If you have fair skin, a history of sunburns, or many moles, Total Body Mapping creates a consistent baseline so your GP can spot changes over time.

blocks.text: Learn more about Total Body Mapping
Skin Check or Total Body Mapping?
blocks.html: Skin Check or Total Body Mapping?
Many patients ask whether they need a standard skin check or Total Body Mapping. The answer depends on your individual circumstances, risk factors and what your GP recommends.
Skin Check

items: Suitable for most adults as part of regular skin cancer monitoring.
Recommended if you have noticed a new, changing or unusual spot.
Your GP examines your skin using a dermatoscope.
Focuses on identifying spots that may need monitoring, biopsy or removal.
Often performed annually, depending on your risk factors.

items: Often helpful for people with many moles, freckles or sun-damaged skin.
Useful when it is difficult to monitor multiple moles over time.
Includes comprehensive photographic imaging alongside your skin check.
Creates a baseline photographic record for future comparison.
May be recommended for people who need closer ongoing skin monitoring.

blocks.text: Why regular skin checks matter in the Redlands
blocks.html: Why regular skin checks matter in the Redlands
Living in bayside suburbs like Victoria Point, Redland Bay and Wellington Point often means a lifetime of sun exposure. Even if you are careful now, many people carry damage from earlier years.
A regular skin check can help your GP:

items: Pick up new or changing spots earlier
Decide which moles need monitoring and which need a closer look
Plan follow up and prevention that fits your personal risk

blocks.html: Finding skin cancer earlier means treatment is more likely to be effective, which is why there is so much emphasis placed on getting checked regularly.

blocks.text: When to book a skin check​
blocks.html: When to book a skin check​
Book a skin cancer check with your GP if any of the following sound familiar:

items: You have not had a full skin check in the last 12 months
You notice a new spot that looks different from your other moles
A mole or spot has changed in size, shape, colour, or feel
You have a sore that does not heal within a few weeks
You have a history of skin cancer, melanoma, or pre-cancerous lesions
You have many moles, very fair skin, a family history of melanoma, or you work outdoors for long periods

blocks.html: Bear in mind, that you do not need to wait to see something that is “obviously worrying”. If you are unsure about that mole or freckle, let your GP check it.

blocks.html: Iron Infusions
At Sunstate Family Practice
Intravenous (IV) iron infusions

An intravenous (IV) iron infusion may be needed to restore iron levels in our body if they fall too low. Why? Because our body depends on iron to function. Iron is used to make haemoglobin – the part of our red blood cells that carries oxygen around our body. It is also important for muscle strength, energy and good mental function. If your iron levels are low, this may make you feel tired and not able to do normal daily activities (Read our article on tiredness and iron deficiency). As the amount of iron in the body falls even lower, the haemoglobin level drops below normal. This is known as iron deficiency anaemia and needs to be treated.
How is iron deficiency treated?

The most common way to treat iron deficiency is to take iron by mouth as a tablet or liquid. This works well for most people and is usually tried first. Some people may need iron to be given straight into the body through a vein. This is called an Intravenous (IV) iron infusion. The iron is given through a needle and dripped (‘infused’) into your vein. Sometimes 2 iron infusions (given at least 1 week apart) are needed to fully top up iron stores. The infusion is made up of iron, not blood.

blocks.text: When might an iron infusion be needed?
blocks.html: When might an iron infusion be needed?
An iron infusion might be needed if you:

items: Are not able to take iron tablets / liquidAre not responding to iron tablets / liquid or not absorbing themNeed to get your iron levels up quickly (eg. before major surgery, late in pregnancy or to avoid blood transfusion)If you have chronic kidney disease or chronic heart failure

title: What is a Sunstate Skin Check? - Sunstate Family Practice
description: Discover what a Sunstate Skin Check involves, a full-body skin cancer screening using advanced dermatoscopy.

blocks.html: Written by Dr Randal Johnson, GP with special interest in skin cancer

Skin cancer remains one of the most common yet preventable forms of cancer in Australia. Early detection through regular skin checks is crucial for effective treatment and better outcomes. At Sunstate Family Practice, we offer a comprehensive Sunstate Skin Check designed to thoroughly examine your skin from head to toe using advanced diagnostic tools.

blocks.text: What Does a Sunstate Skin Check Involve?
blocks.html: What Does a Sunstate Skin Check Involve?

A Sunstate Skin Check involves a meticulous examination of your entire skin surface, including areas that are often overlooked. This is conducted by our experienced general practitioners who have a special interest in skin cancer. The examination uses a dermatoscope, a specialised magnification device equipped with polarising filters that enables the doctor to view subtle changes both on and beneath the surface of your skin.

The dermatoscope enhances the visibility of moles, freckles, and other lesions, helping detect early signs of skin cancer such as melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma. This tool is essential because some dangerous lesions may not be visible to the naked eye or may appear similar to benign spots.

blocks.text: Preparing for Your Skin Check Appointment
blocks.html: Preparing for Your Skin Check Appointment
To ensure an accurate and effective skin examination, there are some important preparations you should make before your appointment:

items: Avoid makeup and sunscreen: Please attend your appointment without any makeup, sunscreen, or moisturisers so that your doctor can clearly see your natural skin condition.
Wear appropriate clothing: You will be asked to remove all clothing except your underwear during the exam. Wearing easily removable clothes can help make this process more comfortable and efficient.
Be ready to discuss your health history: Your doctor will begin by taking a detailed history to understand factors that might increase your risk of developing skin cancer.

blocks.text: Risk Factors Discussed During Your Skin Check
blocks.html: Risk Factors Discussed During Your Skin Check
During the consultation, your doctor will ask about various risk factors including:

items: Sun exposure: Both occupational (work-related) and recreational sun exposure significantly increase the risk of skin damage and skin cancer.
Use of solariums or tanning beds: These artificial sources of UV radiation are known contributors to skin cancer development.
Family history: A family history of melanoma or other skin cancers can raise your personal risk level.
Previous skin cancers or suspicious lesions: If you have had treatment or removal of skin cancers before, this information is vital for ongoing monitoring.

blocks.html: What Happens During the Examination?

Once prepared, you will be asked to sit on the edge of the examination table while the doctor conducts a full-body scan using the dermatoscope. The doctor will carefully inspect all exposed areas of skin, paying particular attention to any spots or lesions that appear unusual or have changed over time.

You should inform your doctor if you have noticed any new, changing, or suspicious spots anywhere on your body—even in areas not routinely examined such as under bras or underwear. While these sites are not always part of the standard check due to privacy reasons, they can still develop serious conditions like melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
Documentation and Follow-Up Care

With your consent, photographs may be taken of certain lesions for documentation purposes. These images allow for precise monitoring over time and help detect any changes early. Your doctor will discuss all findings with you at the end of the appointment and recommend a personalised management plan.
Management options could include:

items: Regular observation with follow-up checks
Medical treatments such as topical therapies
Surgical removal if necessary

blocks.html: Your doctor will also advise when you should schedule your next skin check based on your individual risk profile.

blocks.html: Why Choose Sunstate Family Practice for Your Skin Check?

At Sunstate Family Practice, we prioritise patient comfort alongside clinical excellence. Our doctors are highly trained in identifying early signs of skin cancer and use state-of-the-art equipment to provide the most accurate diagnosis possible.
Regular full skin checks are an important part of skin cancer detection and management and may save your life. Your doctor will discuss with you how frequently you should have your skin checked.

title: How to not get food poisoning during Christmas | Sunstate Family Practice
description: While we don't mind filling up to the brim, don’t let food poisoning ruin your joy. Here’s how to not get food poisoning during Christmas.

blocks.text: It’s that time of the year where every feast looks tempting. Christmas is a time of endless buffets, and while we don’t mind filling up to the brim, we really don’t want to get sick either.
blocks.html: It’s that time of the year where every feast looks tempting. Christmas is a time of endless buffets, and while we don’t mind filling up to the brim, we really don’t want to get sick either.
With 1 out of 5 people at the risk of suffering from bouts of unpleasant symptoms, food poisoning can be a real deal. Here’s what you can do to avoid food poisoning during Christmas.
What is food poisoning?

Foodborne disease, or more commonly food poisoning, is a gastroenteritis condition caused due to food contaminated by bacteria, viruses, or toxins. Once caught, it might cause diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal cramps, vomiting, loss of appetite, and if not, even headaches! Symptoms usually begin as early as 30 minutes and may last up to 7 to 8 weeks, depending on its severity. However, over the festive season, food poisoning is always waiting to happen. For instance, an untouched chocolate fondue is enough to make you a run to the bathroom almost immediately.

And as the summer is heating up even more, we urge taking some simple measures to ensure your food is safe to consume. So, when you forget to take your food inside after a barbeque, you allow the bacteria to multiply over time. And by the time we’re done eating it again, you’re already at risk of suffering from Salmonella food poisoning!

blocks.text: Here are a few tips and tricks to avoid getting sick this festive season.
blocks.html: Here are a few tips and tricks to avoid getting sick this festive season.

blocks.text: 1. Avoid food poisoning by separating raw food from cooked food
blocks.html: 1. Avoid food poisoning by separating raw food from cooked food
One of the most common reasons for food poisoning is failing to separate raw food from cooked food, especially when it’s meat, such as poultry.
Salmonella outbreaks are often caused when consuming raw or uncooked food, such as adding undercooked eggs in a brilliant salad.
Considering that a salad usually goes into the fridge after a meal, you might forget it this time because, hey! it’s a festive time, and we’re all swamped.
2. Thaw food into the fridge
Storage of food at the right temperature is as important as preparing it.
Ensure you keep hot food items warm on top of the stove, covered, or in the oven. And when it comes to something like cakes, or puddings, keep it inside the fridge.

blocks.text: 3. Food handling should be at its best
blocks.html: 3. Food handling should be at its best

Maintaining proper food hygiene is incredibly important. Make sure you wash your hands before handling food. Wash knives, chopping boards, and utensils after use, and use separate chopping boards for raw meats and vegetables to avoid cross-contamination.

blocks.text: 4. Don’t try cooking if you’re not well
blocks.html: 4. Don’t try cooking if you’re not well
We recommend not preparing food for others if you’ve symptoms of gastroenteritis until 48 hours after symptoms have passed.
5. Follow cooking instructions

When preparing food from packages, follow the instructions. You might have to set the appliance at a different temperature or probably give an extra wash to your poultry, or avoid mixing a marinade directly onto your cooked food.

blocks.text: 6. Do not forget to cover your meals once cooked
blocks.html: 6. Do not forget to cover your meals once cooked
It will not just retain the heat, but also prevent contamination from air.
7. Take extra care with leftovers

Make sure that the left-overs are stored in sealed containers right away in the fridge or freezer to retain their freshness. Remember, we are trying to avoid contamination at all costs! Consume the left-over not more than two days.

blocks.text: And finally, an overstocked fridge can stop hot foods from cooling properly. So use this as a guide and be mindful of how you serve and store your food to ensure no one in the family ruins their festive season with bouts of unpleasant food poisoning.

title: Thyroid Health- The often overlooked gland | Thyroid Disorder | GP Care
description: Thyroid disorder can wreak havoc to almost everything, from skin to your mood. Read our article on why thyroid health shouldn’t be overlooked.

blocks.text: Chances are you will probably never think about your thyroid health until you suffer from a disorder that can wreak havoc to almost everything – from your skin to your mood and even your sleep!
blocks.html: Chances are you will probably never think about your thyroid health until you suffer from a disorder that can wreak havoc to almost everything – from your skin to your mood and even your sleep!

Thyroid health rarely gets the limelight of more well-known areas like heart health or lung health, yet a thyroid disorder can also lead to fatal consequences. In fact, an estimated 60 percent of people with some form of thyroid disorder don’t know they have one.
It is a small “butterfly-shaped” gland that forms the body’s endocrine systemand virtually influencing every other organ in the body.

The thyroid gland is responsible for a wide variety of functions. It sets the body’s pace that affects how fast or slow your brain works, heart, muscles, liver and even how nice you feel about yourself. It keeps the body’s metabolism under control through the action of thyroid hormones, which it produces by extracting iodine from the blood.

And because the thyroid gland influences a variety of body functions, it is important to seek medical help if any problems arise. And if you notice symptoms of thyroid disorders, be sure to get tested and examined by a doctor.

blocks.text: What are the different types of thyroid disorders?
blocks.html: What are the different types of thyroid disorders?
Thyroid disorders can range from a small, harmless goitre, which is nothing but an engraved thyroid gland to causing fatal cancers.
It starts and involves the abnormal production of thyroid hormones, namely T3 and T4 hormones that can result in two different conditions.

In case, when the thyroid produces too many of these hormones, it causes a medical condition that uses energy very quickly. It leads to causing persistent tiredness and unexplained weight loss even when not trying to. This is called hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid).

On the other hand, when the gland produces lesser hormones, it is called a condition called hypothyroidism (underactive) that causes increased weight gain and mightleave you very sensitive to cold temperature.

blocks.text: What are the signs and symptoms to watch out for?
blocks.html: What are the signs and symptoms to watch out for?

blocks.alt: A man holding his neck due to thyroid disorder pain, thyroid health, GP in Victoria point

blocks.text: Symptoms to watch out for hyperthyroidism
blocks.html: Symptoms to watch out for hyperthyroidism

items: Facing trouble concentrating at work and studies
Unusually sensitive to warm conditions
Having irregular and fast heart rate
Feeling irritable and nervous
Losing weight without trying
Sleeplessness
Diarrhea

blocks.text: Symptoms to watch out for hypothyroidism
blocks.html: Symptoms to watch out for hypothyroidism

items: Feeling cold even when others are comfortable
Feeling exhausted without any strenuous work
Having a slower heart rate than usual
Suffering from constipation
Unexplained weight gain
Dry skin

blocks.html: Diagnosis of thyroid disorders
When a thyroid disorder is suspected, your GP will usually start your diagnosis with thyroid blood tests and additional testings for confirmation.

When diagnosing thyroid disorders, your clinician will assess the pituitary gland – thyroid gland relationship. This is done by measuring the levels of thyroid hormones – T3 and T4 hormones in your blood, as well as TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) blood levels.
Since thyroid disorders are widely overlooked and underdiagnosed, it is crucial to talk to your doctors about screening. A simple blood test can confirm if your thyroid gland is working fine.

title: Women’s Health Week 2020: Recognising women’s mental and physical health - Sunstate Family Practice
description: We encourage all women in our community to focus on their medical needs and take time to check on their health regularly.

blocks.html: Women’s health week is one of Australia’s biggest awareness events focused on maintaining and wellbeing for all women and girls. This yearly event held by Jean Hailes encourages women and girls to learn more about their health requirements and medical needs to improve their health by making the right choices. This Women’s Health Week, we at Sunstate Family Practice encourage all women in our community to focus on their medical needs and take time to check on their health regularly.
Why does women's health matter?

In this time of global pandemic and juggling professional and personal life, women’s health has never been more important. It doesn’t only include taking care of physical health, but mental wellbeing is also vital for a woman’s overall good health.

Women can also play a crucial role in maintaining a family’s health. And, as such, they can quite often start neglecting their own health needs. Therefore, it is imperative for women to take the time to look after themselves and visit their doctors regularly.
Never miss your health checks
According to The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, there has been a significant drop in the number of female attendees due to the ongoing COVID-19 crisis.
Even in the most difficult times, it is important for every woman to recognise their physical and mental health needs and not miss or delay any health screenings.

Cardiovascular diseases for example are a major threat to the health of Australia women, affecting over two million Australia women at any given time. However, most of these health threats are always preventable- if you do it.
Talking with your health providers is the best way to understand your risks and prevent diseases. All women must be well informed about their health risks, the facts and not ignore any mental issues.

blocks.text: Manage health threats through regular screenings
blocks.html: Manage health threats through regular screenings

blocks.alt: A female patient consulting her nurse during her regular health checks, Woman's Doctor Brisbane

blocks.html: Blood tests, cholesterol screenings, mammograms and Pap smears are only some of the regular health checks important for women’s healthy wellbeing.

If you diligently follow your health schedules with experts, it can make a big difference in your life. For example, women diagnosed with breast cancer can successfully recover with early treatment that is only possible if the cancer is detected in an early stage.

blocks.text: Important health screenings every woman should do.
blocks.html: Important health screenings every woman should do.

blocks.alt: A woman checking her health stats with a help of a regular blood test, Woman's doctors Brisbane

blocks.html: Blood test
A simple blood test can reveal a lot on your health – how well your organs are functioning, diagnose diseases including infections, cancer, coronary heart conditions and many more.
In fact, blood tests help in identifying potential conditions early that help your doctor to start a management plan, treatments and medications that can work best for you.
Blood pressure and cholesterol checks
If you have diabetes, heart diseases or any other certain medical conditions, having your blood pressure checked at least once in a year is recommended.

Cholesterol screenings are tools to detect and assess your risks for heart disease and stroke. An abnormal level of cholesterol puts you at risk for heart disease. In this case, consult your doctor who can initiate a management plan to prevent or mitigate your risks.
Every woman at the age of 45 should start regular blood screenings and consult local GPs to prepare a roadmap to good health.
Diabetes Screenings
Again starting at the age of 45, every woman should get regular blood glucose tests, at least once every two years to check for diabetes and prediabetes.

If you’re obese or if you have other risks such as if you have a first-degree relative diagnosed with diabetes or a family history of heart diseases then you should have more frequent diabetes screenings.
Breast cancer screening

Early detection of breast cancer through mammograms is crucial to saving your life from the disease. Screenings can detect early signs of abnormalities, ensuring that your doctor gets enough time to decide on your treatment plans and help you recover as quickly as possible.

According to BreastScreen Australia, women aged 50-74 should undergo a screening mammogram every two years, whereas women aged between 40 to 49 or 75 or older should seek help from their GPs and decide on how often screening is required.
Bone health check

When you get older, visiting regular bone density tests for screening osteoporosis is recommended. With early identification of low bone density, medical assistance, medications, lifestyle changes and therapies can help protect your bone health and reduce the risks for fractures.

blocks.text: Choose a healthier lifestyle and make health a priority
blocks.html: Choose a healthier lifestyle and make health a priority

While it is impossible to entirely eliminate all your health risks, choosing to adapt to a new healthier lifestyle is definitely beneficial. Quitting or reducing smoking, choosing vegetables over processed food or getting more active are some ways to control most risks.

If you’re stressed and not in a healthy mental state, seek help from GPs. GPs can be your first port of call for managing stress and chronic mental issues, and can refer you to specialists or other allied health professionals for further treatment if required.
This Women’s Health Week, we encourage all women in our community to focus on your medical needs and take time to check on your health regularly.

blocks.html: Pandemic is Greek for everywhere and everybody, so if a pandemic comes to pass then everyone in Australia will be affected in some way by the disease. It does not mean everyone will get it, but you may know somebody who does or have your work disrupted, or have to care for someone who has it. It is highly infectious but almost everyone recovers.

The main problem with a disease like this is the possibility that a lot of the population is sick and recovering at the same time, affecting workplaces, the economy and putting a strain on essential services.
The extremes of age, young and elderly, and patients with chronic illness are more prone to complications.

I posted a short time ago, that we would not be seeing patients that we suspected of having coronavirus, however as this has now become a pandemic that may now not be possible. We may have lost the battle for containment.
With that in mind as the principal doctor at Sunstate Family Practice, I would like patients of the practice to read and act on the following:

items: Patients with chronic disease, who are on multiple medications, need to ensure that your scripts are up to date. You do not, repeat do not need to stock up on medication but you do need to ensure that if your scripts are coming due that you come and see us sooner rather than later to do this, and have enough at home to last for a month.

If you have a chronic disease and you have let it go a bit, see a doctor soon to ensure that it is managed as tightly as possible, before you may potentially get sick. The best defense against coronavirus is to be as healthy as possible before you get it. Manage any chronic conditions well, eat well including protein, stay hydrated, do some cardiovascular exercise. Do this all before you get sick.
People who have chronic lung disease and asthma particularly need to pay attention to the above and have a current action plan, set of puffers, and scripts for more going forward.
If you are a smoker – QUIT NOW, big ask I know but worthwhile.

The same applies to routine referral, blood tests, etc. Come in and get any regular needs sorted soon. These steps are to avoid you having to come for routine but important things when many other people including doctors may be sick, and it may be harder to find an appointment.

People with chronic immunodeficiency diseases, cancer, are currently on chemotherapeutic medication, have chronic autoimmune diseases and or taking immunosuppressive medication. If you need to see us here for a medical reason do this as a matter of urgency. As it would be far better for you to be seen before the pandemic hits in full force.

There is no vaccination against coronavirus, however, when the seasonal flu vaccination becomes available we will be advising patients to make use of this even more than last year. The flu is not related to coronavirus and the flu vaccination does not affect the coronavirus however these sorts of new viruses such as coronavirus, SARS, etc are much more dangerous when coupled to other medical conditions. Having coronavirus and the flu concurrently would be a significant concern.

The latest published figures indicate a mortality rate of up to 3.8%. Compare this with the seasonal flu which has a mortality rate of less than 0.1%. It is our job as medical officers to try and reduce to try and reduce that number as much as possible, and identify the patients most at risk. As this pandemic evolves, you may find that there may be disruptions to your normal appointments or your normal doctor may be isolated seeing sick people. I would ask that you please bear with us as we deal with this developing situation.

In regards to whether SFP will become a testing center for the disease, we have not yet decided as we are waiting on protective equipment to be provided to the staff for this to occur. We will let patients know when we do.

This sort of post will be the first of many that we will need to do, so, please if you are reading this and you know other patients of the practice, please share and get them to follow us here on Facebook. This post is designed to be informative for patients to take sensible steps before the pandemic hits. When it does, we will need to pass the information on to patients quickly so please follow us on Facebook as it is the most efficient way.

title: Being a GP in the current Coronavirus world - Dr Amy Heales - March 2020
description: Many people have asked me what it’s like being a GP in the current Coronavirus world. So I thought I’d try and describe it.

blocks.html: Many people have asked me what it’s like being a GP in the current Coronavirus world. So I thought I’d write something to try and describe it ( and also for personal therapy… “journaling” I believe the professionals call it )

When I got home from work earlier in the week, and my husband asked how my day was, I honestly couldn’t describe it. It doesn’t happen often, but I couldn’t find the words. So I just said “it’s indescribable”.<u></u><u></u>

Later on that night while lying in bed, I thought of the patients I had seen in the day. My first patient was the manager of a local grocery store. Stress level through the roof as you can imagine. I don’t know how she was managing to keep it together to be honest!<u></u><u></u>

Next, I saw a young mum with a new bub who told me about what social distancing meant for her. Basically, she was stuck at home and feeling more isolated than what she already was with a newborn. Her mother’s group had been cancelled, birthday parties cancelled, she decided it was too risky to go to the shops.<u></u><u></u>

But probably the thing she was most sad about was not visiting her mum and dad. She wanted to protect her parents from getting sick. I encouraged her and assured her she was doing the right thing.<u></u><u></u>
I saw three patients with sore throats who were worried about Coronavirus. I told them the risk is low but unfortunately we can’t test you. So you must stay at home until you are well.<u></u><u></u>

I haven’t worn a mask for 6 years, but I wore a mask for half the day… I apologised profusely to my patients because I felt like it broke down our communication. But everyone was ok with it.<u></u><u></u>

My lovely 75 year old patient came in and told me she had a fever 2 weeks ago, and a cough and was still feeling tired. She had stayed at home since she first got sick to be cautious and was wondering how much longer she had to stay there. I sadly told her she had to stay inside until she was well. I knew this patient didn’t have family nearby so I asked her if someone could drop her some supplies if she was in need. She told me her neighbours had been checking on her and would help her out thank goodness. I’m going to call her later in the week and see how she’s going.<u></u><u></u>

I had a lady who told me all their bookings for their family owned business had been cancelled for the coming months so they had no income. One lady asked me if she should go to a funeral for a friend.. I had to say no. My patient who was already struggling with anxiety told me she was really not coping at the moment.<u></u><u></u>

Every patient in my day had a story.. A worry. A concern. A corona related question..
The hardest part for me was not being able to answer them all with clear cut answers. Medicine is sometimes black and white , and sometimes medicine is grey. And this corona thing is well and truly parked in the grey area. For a little while at least.

Still not sure how to describe it all but there is a few things that stand out. Firstly, how much appreciation I have for my colleagues. Our receptionists, our nurses, our practices managers and fellow doctors. And everyone out there in GP land who I know is going through the same stuff as us. It’s the small things we do every day that will “Flatten the curve”. We got this!<u></u><u></u>

I felt really privileged to be in the position to help people to make sense of this crazy world at the moment. It’s hard to do this when, as doctors , we aren’t sure what’s going on and things are constantly changing.<u></u><u></u>

But I educated my patients on self isolation, on symptoms, on testing, on protecting the elderly, on infection control. I reminded them about being aware of their mental health and the seek help if they are feeling anxious or depressed. We had minimal training in how to deal with a pandemic at medical school, so I’m sort of just winging it and hoping I’m making a difference.<u></u><u></u>

While every patient I saw today had a different story or concern, one thing was constant among them- not one of them complained. Not one took offence to me wearing a mask, or asking them to wash their hands. I went first and then it was their turn. And then we laughed a little at how crazy it all was…<u></u><u></u>

Thank you to all of these wonderful patients for your kindness and your understanding. It goes a long way and is greatly appreciated. Spread that kindness far and wide, god knows we need it at the moment!<u></u><u></u>
In this crazy time, when words can’t be found to describe how we are all feeling, it was the words from one of my patients on that day that stuck with me…<u></u><u></u>
I said “I’m so sorry I have to wear a mask today and sit so far away” …<u></u><u></u>
And she replied.. “Don’t worry Dr Heales, we are all in this together”<u></u><u></u>
And I thought- never was a truer word spoken.<u></u><u></u>
We are all in this together

title: Dr Matt Harvey - Covid-19 Preparedness and self-isolation [Mar 23, 2020]
description: On March 23, 2020, we asked Dr. Matt Harvey at Sunstate Family Practice to respond to your Coronavirus FAQs. 12 Questions, 12 Answers.

blocks.html: We asked Dr. Matt Harvey to respond to some of your Coronavirus FAQ…
1. Are we safe to visit?

Yes, you are safe to visit us. We have increased cleaning and made some changes in the practice to improve safety for our patients and for our team. The waiting room looks a bit different, and the people on the front desk might direct you to sit in a particular place, and they will ask you to wash your hands and maintain safe spaces between yourself and other people in the waiting room.

If you, your child, or someone you’re caring for are unwell with fever or cough or breathing problems, please phone us first on 3207-7744 before coming in. We might need to ask you to wait in your car before a doctor sees you. To maintain safety, we have designated doctors and staff members to see unwell people on different days, so you may not get to see your usual doctor, but rest assured that all of our doctors will take good care of you, and they all work together as a team. They can speak with your usual doctor to clarify and longstanding issues if needed.

blocks.text: 2. Should I be tested for COVID-19?
blocks.html: 2. Should I be tested for COVID-19?

The Government currently has in place strict testing criteria that determine who can be tested. This is to preserve the testing resources needed to manage the pandemic in the longer term. The Government will change the testing criteria from time to time as needed. If you’re well, you don’t need to be tested. If you have any symptoms, please ring us to discuss your concerns. You might be eligible for a telephone consultation with one of our doctors.

blocks.text: 3. Should I reschedule my routine appointment?
blocks.html: 3. Should I reschedule my routine appointment?

If you are well, there is no need to reschedule your appointment. The pandemic is going to be around for several months. In that time, it’s really important to attend to your routine health care to stay well.
If you are unwell at the time of your routine appointment, please call us ahead of time to discuss whether you need to reschedule or change the purpose of your appointment,
4. Should I delay immunizations?

If you and your children are well, there is no need to delay immunizations. In fact, it is more important than ever right now to make sure all of your own and your children’s immunizations are up to date, especially for Influenza, whooping cough and pneumococcal disease.
If you or your children are unwell, please call us to plan what needs to be done.

blocks.text: 5. When can I have a flu injection & will this protect me against COVID-19?
blocks.html: 5. When can I have a flu injection & will this protect me against COVID-19?

Our stocks of flu immunizations have just started to come in and our priority in the next couple of weeks is getting people with more severe health problems to be immunized first. If you have heart or lung conditions, immune system problems, cancer, or you are over 65 years old, we want to see you soon! If you’re otherwise well it’s still ok to wait a little while and book in with us after Easter.
We will be running immunization clinics regularly. In those clinics, the doctor will also talk to you about any other immunizations that you might need.

Unfortunately, the flu immunization won’t protect you against COVID-19. But it’s really important to still get the flu needle this year because it’s possible to be infected with influenza and coronavirus at the same time, and we need to prevent that from happening to anyone.

blocks.text: 6. My family member has been tested, should I self-isolate?
blocks.html: 6. My family member has been tested, should I self-isolate?
Yes.

Please self-isolate until the test results are known. If your family member tests negative then you can re-enter the community. If your family member tests positive then you will need to self isolate for 14 days. Please call us if you start becoming unwell or have any other concerns during that time. You will be eligible for a Medicare-funded telephone consultation with your doctor.

blocks.text: 7. I have a cough, but nothing else. Should I come in?
blocks.html: 7. I have a cough, but nothing else. Should I come in?

No, not yet. The best thing you can do right now stays home, rest, stay well hydrated and well-nourished. If you have asthma or any other lung or heart conditions please call us for further advice. If your symptoms are getting worse rather than better after 2 or 3 days, please call us for further advice.
8. When should I self-isolate?

If you are unwell with cough, fever or other cold and flu symptoms. If you have a health condition that puts you at risk of severe complications from COVID -19, eg. heart and lung conditions, immune system problems, cancer, and advanced age.

Please remember if you are self-isolating because you are at risk, it is still important to attend to your regular health care needs. It is still safe to come out to see us, but please phone us first to choose the best time.

blocks.text: 9. When should I stop my parents from visiting my children?
blocks.html: 9. When should I stop my parents from visiting my children?
Now.

We know that children who catch coronavirus generally only experience mild symptoms, so the risk to children individually is generally considered to be low at this stage. Older adults tend to experience more severe symptoms and are at higher risk of dying from coronavirus. Younger children often find it difficult to understand the need for maintaining safe distances and older children may forget to maintain safe spaces, wash their hands, cough into their elbows and so forth.

blocks.text: 10. How do we stay sane and healthy during this time?
blocks.html: 10. How do we stay sane and healthy during this time?

These are difficult and uncertain times and quite stressful for most of us. It is important to maintain the connection with friends and family over the phone, online and with video platforms like Skype or Zoom. If you have to self isolate, make sure you plan and stick to a routine throughout your day. Pick up an old hobby you used to enjoy, or try something new! It’s safe to go outside and go for a walk with the dog, do some work in your yard, take the kids to the park and so forth, just as long as we all remember to maintain safe spaces from one another.
If you are experiencing severe mental distress, you can speak to your GP and ring services like Lifeline or Beyond Blue. Some psychologists may also be able to provide support over the phone.
11. Should I go visit friends?

You can visit friends if everyone is well with no fever or respiratory symptoms and if everyone maintains safe spaces. It’s best to try to find an outdoor space where you can meet, and keep the gathering small.
12. Can we go outside?

Yes, absolutely! We should all be getting some outside time for fresh air and exercise. If you’re unwell, you can still go out in your yard or on a balcony. If you have no access to an enclosed space and have to use communal spaces, maintain a good distance from other people and wear a mask if possible. If you’re well, you can go outside to public spaces as long as the area isn’t too crowded and you can easily maintain a 2-meter space from other people.
____________________________________

This information is of a general nature only. It may not apply to your individual circumstances. It is not intended to substitute for medical advice. For further information and specific advice please contact Sunstate Family Practice on 3207 7744 or after hours, the National Coronavirus Health Information Line on 1800 020 080

title: A Simple Skin Check Could Save You Big Time - Sunstate Family Practice
description: How UV rays cause damage, what to expect in a skin check, and how Total Body Mapping helps detect early changes.

blocks.html: Did you know? Late spring is actually one of the best times of the year for a skin check.
Your skin is naturally lighter after winter, which makes any new or changing spots easier for doctors to see, including those that might have developed from sun exposure last summer.
At Sunstate Family Practice in Victoria Point, our doctors make skin checks simple, thorough and comfortable, and we also offer Total Body Mapping (TBM) to take your care one step further.
This article covers:

items: How UV rays actually damage the skin and increase cancer risk
What to expect during a professional skin check
How Total Body Mapping (TBM) helps detect even the smallest
changes early
Sun-smart tips: Knowing is power

blocks.html: How the Sun Damages Skin
Sunlight is made up of invisible ultraviolet (UV) rays. These rays penetrate the skin and can damage the DNA in your skin cells.
Sunlight contains two types of ultraviolet (UV) rays: UVA and UVB:

items: UVB rays cause sunburn and can damage DNA, increasing the risk of skin cancer
UVA rays penetrate deeper into the skin, contributing to premature ageing, wrinkles, and also playing a role in skin cancer

blocks.html: Over time, that damage can build up and cause cells to grow in abnormal ways, and that’s how skin cancer begins.
It’s not just about sunburn. Even mild, repeated exposure can cause tiny changes beneath the surface that aren’t visible straight away.
In fact, many skin cancers appear months or even years after the damage first occurs.
Regular skin checks are one of the smartest habits you can have when it comes to health, especially if you live somewhere sunny like Victoria Point, Redland Bay or Cleveland.
We’ve heard it before, but it’s nothing to roll your eyes at: Queensland has the highest rate of skin cancer in Australia, and Australia has one of the highest rates in the world.
Take a look at these skin cancer facts by SunSmart, which don’t tell a very nice story. E.g. “More than two in three Australians will be diagnosed with skin cancer in their lifetime”.

blocks.text: Skin Checks With Total Body Mapping
blocks.html: Skin Checks With Total Body Mapping

A skin check is quick, non-invasive and done in complete privacy. During your appointment, your doctor will examine areas of your skin looking for moles, freckles, or spots that have changed in colour, size or shape.
Total Body Mapping (TBM) adds another layer of accuracy, and it’s available at Sunstate Family Practice for good reason.
Using high-quality medical imaging, it creates a full photographic record of your skin. This allows doctors to compare images over time.

It’s safe, confidential, and ideal for anyone with lots of moles, fair skin, or a family history of melanoma. Think of TBM as your personal skin health archive, it makes future checks faster, clearer and more reassuring.

FYI: “Total” doesn’t mean 100% total, it means the areas that get, or have got sun exposure, like your face, arms, legs, neck and possibly your back, among others. We only check and photograph areas that we discuss with you prior.
You can certainly show/tell your doctor areas you’ve noticed that have sun damage too.

blocks.text: What Happens During a Skin Check
blocks.html: What Happens During a Skin Check

items: Your GP will ask about your medical and sun exposure history
Then your GP checks pre-discussed areas of your skin, possibly using a dermatoscope
If any spots look suspicious, your doctor may photograph or monitor them, or arrange a biopsy for further testing
Your doctor will discuss the findings with you, and recommend the next steps

blocks.html: The appointment usually takes between 15–30 minutes, and most people leave feeling relieved and more in control of their health.

blocks.text: Sun-smart tips: Knowing is Power for Everyday Skin Protection
blocks.html: Sun-smart tips: Knowing is Power for Everyday Skin Protection
1.What SPF really means:
SPF 50+ doesn’t mean 50 minutes of protection or 50% shade.
SPF, or Sun Protection Factor, measures how much UVB radiation a sunscreen blocks.

items: SPF 30 can block about 97% of UVB rays
SPF 50 can blocks about 98% of UVB rays

blocks.html: That’s right: SPF 50 isn’t “20 points” better than SPF 30.
Higher SPF gives slightly more protection, but only if you apply enough per the instructions.
For best results, use broad-spectrum sunscreen (it protects against UVA and UVB).
2. Check the CHOICE sunscreen guide:
See how your brand performs in real-world conditions take a look at the CHOICE Sunscreen Test.
3. Understand the UV index:
Anything above 3 means UV levels are high enough to cause skin damage. You can check this in your weather app before heading out.
The scale goes to 11+ (max), and there are plenty of days in Queensland that hit those extremes.
Don’t think clouds are your friends. On a cloudy day, over 90% of UV rays can still get through, and sometimes patchy clouds can even increase UV levels due to reflection and concentration.
4. Watch reflective surfaces:
Sand, concrete, and water can reflect up to 80% of UV rays, increasing exposure even in the shade.
For better protection, apply sunscreen:

items: Eyelids
Under the chin and jawline
On the underside of your arms

blocks.html: 5. Don’t forget your eyes:
UV rays can damage the surface of your eyes too, but sunglasses with UV400 protection can help prevent cataracts and sun-related eye conditions.
It can harm the cornea and lens over time, leading to blurry vision, eye ageing, and even macular damage. Take a look here for more information on that.
Choose your sunnies wisely!

blocks.text: At The End of The Day
blocks.html: At The End of The Day
Regular skin checks are more than just a precaution.
They’re a simple, effective way to stay ahead of skin damage and protect your long-term health.

With late spring being a perfect time to spot changes, and tools like Total Body Photography making checks even more accurate and reassuring, there’s never been a better moment to prioritise your skin.
Take charge of your skin health today, gain peace of mind, and step into summer confidently.

title: Skin Changes With Age: What’s Normal and What Needs Checking - Sunstate Family Practice
description: Which skin changes are normal with age and what to watch for. Sunstate Family Practice offers skin checks and Total Body Mapping (TBM).

blocks.html: Everyone’s skin changes gradually over time, so some changes are easy to miss.

A new spot on your arm, a mole that looks darker than usual, or skin that feels thinner than last year may seem minor, but noticing these differences early can affect how quickly it can be assessed and managed if needed.
Many changes are harmless, but some are worth checking.
What’s in this article

items: How skin naturally changes with age
Normal skin changes to expect
Red flags to watch for
Comparing moles and lesions
How Total Body Mapping (TBM) can help

blocks.html: How skin changes with age
Skin is our largest organ and is constantly renewing itself, so over time, natural changes occur.
Skin becomes thinner, less elastic, the tone may vary, and healing can be slower.
These shifts happen due to a combination of genetics, hormones, and environmental factors such as sun exposure.
For example, someone who spends a lot of time on the beach may notice small, flat patches on their hands or shoulders from accumulated sun exposure.
Others may see subtle sagging around the jawline or fine lines around the eyes.
Most age‑related spots are benign, but new or changing lesions should be assessed if you are unsure.

Normal skin changes
Some changes are part of the natural ageing process and usually harmless. Here are some common examples:
Fine lines and wrinkles:Appear where skin stretches most, such as around the eyes and mouth, caused by gradual collagen loss.
Dryness and rough texture:Less oil production leads to slightly rougher skin, especially on arms and legs.
Age spots:Small, flat patches from sun exposure over the years, commonly seen on hands, shoulders, and face.
Mild sagging:Loss of firmness around the jawline or upper arms is common.

Slower healing:Minor scratches or cuts take longer to repair.
These changes are generally predictable and do not require urgent medical attention, but noticing them helps you track what is normal for your skin.

Red flags to watch
Some changes should be checked sooner rather than later. These include:
New or changing moles:Look for spots that grow quickly, change shape, develop uneven colour, or have irregular borders. Even small changes over a few weeks to months can be significant.
Use the ABCDE + ‘ugly duckling’ method:Doctors often use the ABCDE rule (Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter, Evolving) and the ‘ugly duckling’ sign — a spot that looks different from your others.
Persistent sores or itchy spots:Any sore, scab, or lesion that does not heal within two to three weeks should be assessed.
Lumps, thickened patches, or crusty areas:These can sometimes represent skin cancers or other conditions that need assessment.
Sudden pigmentation changes:Dark patches, redness around a mole, or new streaks of colour can indicate a problem. Even changes in freckles or areas of long-standing sun damage should be checked.
Add nodular melanoma caution:Some fast‑growing melanomas may appear as a firm, raised, evenly coloured lump — any rapidly growing new lesion should be checked.
If you notice any of these signs, consider booking a skin check with your GP.
The GPs at Sunstate Family Practice may recommend monitoring, further investigation, or procedures depending on the findings.
If something needs treatment, earlier assessment can sometimes mean simpler treatment options.
Comparing normal and suspicious moles
Normal moles are usually symmetrical, even in col our, and stay fairly consistent over time. Suspicious moles may:

items: Change in size, shape, or colour over weeks or months
Develop uneven edges or multiple shades
Appear raised or start bleeding or itching

blocks.html: If you see any of these changes, even if subtle, it is time to book a skin check.

blocks.text: What to do if you’re not sure
blocks.html: What to do if you’re not sure
“Did that always look like that?” It’s a question many people ask themselves.
A good idea is to make a note in your phone, ideally with a few photos, and compare changes over time. Keep images private and bring them to your GP rather than sharing online.
If you notice anything suspicious, or aren’t sure, a simple skin check can confirm whether action needs to be taken, and offer peace of mind.
Sunstate Family Practice offers comprehensive skin checks and optional Total Body Mapping for higher‑risk patients.

Total Body Mapping (TBM)helps create a visual record of your skin over time. Using precise imaging, TBM captures moles, freckles, and lesions from consistent angles and lighting, making it easier to compare changes between visits.
TBM is particularly helpful if you have a large number of moles, fair skin, a history of sun exposure, or a personal or family history of melanoma.
Your GP can advise whether TBM is appropriate for your risk level.
It can help document areas that are hard to see yourself, such as the back, shoulders, and scalp.
After your appointment, your GP will discuss what to watch for and when review may be recommended.
TBM is an adjunct to, not a replacement for, a clinical skin examination.

title: Why Continuity of Care Matters: Seeing the Same GP Over Time - Sunstate Family Practice
description: What continuity of care really means and why seeing the same GP over time helps families in Victoria Point and the Redlands areas.

blocks.html: Visiting a doctor can sometimes feel like starting with a blank slate, especially when it’s someone new.
Every GP sees you at a single point in time, but your health evolves over months and years. For example, energy levels change, skin patterns shift, sleep and stress habits fluctuate.
Observing these changes is easier when your GP knows your story, rather than piecing it together from scratch each visit.
That’s where continuity of care comes in.
What’s in this article

items: What continuity of care means in everyday life
Why repeating your health story can hide patterns
How families and children benefit from a familiar GP
Why local, long-term care makes a practical difference

blocks.text: What continuity of care means (in real life)
blocks.html: What continuity of care means (in real life)

Continuity of care is about having a GP who gets to know you and your specifics. That means understanding what’s typical for you, your family’s health history, and how your lifestyle fits into the picture.
Over time, your GP starts to see your health as a story, not a series of separate visits.
Small changes become easier to spot because there’s context behind them. A dip in energy, a change in sleep, or a skin concern isn’t just viewed in isolation.
It’s seen as part of what’s been happening over months or years.
For many people, that shared understanding makes appointments feel less rushed and more focused.
The independent GPs at Sunstate Family Practice all have long lists of patients who see them time and time again for this reason.
Re‑explaining your health
Your GP needs to learn what matters most about your health, any relevant family history, what’s been tried before, and what tends to work for you.
Gradual changes can sound minor when they’re described as single moments.
Recurring issues can seem unrelated when they’re actually connected.
Having the same GP means those patterns don’t rely on memory alone. This is another reason why many patients opt for our Total Body Mapping (TBM) services too, which documents changes over time.
Over time, your doctor becomes familiar with how you usually feel when you’re well, which makes it easier to recognise when something has shifted.

blocks.text: Why continuity of care matters for families and children
blocks.html: Why continuity of care matters for families and children
For parents, continuity of care can be especially valuable. A GP who’s followed a child’s development over time has a clearer sense of what’s new and what’s part of a longer pattern.
That can make conversations about growth, behaviour, sleep, or recurring illness more meaningful.

There’s also the emotional side. Going to the doctor can feel daunting for younger children. Seeing a familiar face in the room can make appointments feel safer and more predictable, which often leads to better communication and less stress for everyone involved.
Vaccinations are another area where continuity of care really helps. A familiar face can really help take the edge off nerves in kids.
For adults, the same idea applies. Seeing the same person, and putting a face to a name can make it easier to talk openly about changes you might otherwise brush aside.

blocks.alt: Child and doctor

blocks.text: Local care that understands local life
blocks.html: Local care that understands local life
Victoria Point and the surrounding Redlands area are full of active, outdoor lifestyles, family routines, and community connections.
A GP who knows this local context can better notice subtle changes in your health over time, because they understand how local lifestyle, environment, and routines influence your wellbeing.

At Sunstate Family Practice, continuity of care is supported by tools like Total Body Mapping (TBM), which tracks skin changes across months and years. This approach helps catch issues early and ensures care is based on what’s genuinely changing, not just what’s visible in a single visit.

blocks.text: Choosing a GP, not just an appointment
blocks.html: Choosing a GP, not just an appointment

Booking a medical visit is often about finding a time that fits your day. But over the long run, choosing a GP who gets to know you and your family can make those visits more useful and more reassuring.
Sunstate Family Practice welcomes patients seeking that kind of ongoing relationship with their doctor.
You can book online or call the practice to schedule with your preferred GP and start building care that carries forward, visit by visit.

title: What Happens When Your GP Finds a Suspicious Spot?
description: Monitoring, biopsy or removal? A Victoria Point GP explains what happens after a suspicious spot is found at your skin check — and when to book a review.

blocks.html: Your GP pauses at one spot during your skin check and takes a closer look. What happens from there?

Spots don’t automatically need to be removed. Depending on what your GP sees, you may be advised that no further action is currently required, have an area monitored for changes, or need further investigation, such as a skin biopsy.
This article covers

items:
When a spot is monitored
What a skin biopsy involves
When removal is recommended
How ongoing monitoring works

blocks.text: Three possible outcomes after a skin check
blocks.html: Three possible outcomes after a skin check
No further action recommended at this appointment

Your GP has not identified a spot requiring further investigation based on the examination performed at that appointment. Continue to monitor your skin and seek medical advice if you notice a new or changing spot.
Monitoring recommended
A spot has characteristics your GP wants to monitor. Images may be taken so its size, shape, colour or other features can be compared at a future appointment.
Further investigation or treatment
Your GP may recommend a biopsy or removal based on the appearance of the spot and your individual circumstances.

blocks.text: What factors can affect your skin cancer risk?
blocks.html: What factors can affect your skin cancer risk?

Age is only one part of skin cancer risk. Skin type, previous sun exposure, outdoor work, family history, previous skin cancers, solarium use, and certain medical conditions or medicines can also affect a person’s risk.
Cancer Council Australia provides a detailed overview ofrecognised skin cancer risk factors.
Skin cancer risk is influenced by a combination of factors. These may include:

items: fair or sun-sensitive skin
a history of significant sunburn or extensive sun exposure
outdoor work or recreation
numerous or unusual-looking moles
a personal or family history of melanoma or other skin cancers
previous suspicious skin lesions
solarium use
medicines or medical conditions that suppress the immune system.

blocks.html: Having one or more of these factors does not mean that you have or will develop skin cancer. People without these factors can also develop skin cancer.
Your GP can consider your individual history and examine your skin before recommending whether you need further assessment, ongoing skin checks or photographic monitoring.
New or changing spots, or spots that concern you, should be assessed regardless of your risk factors.
If you are concerned about a new or changing spot,book an appointment with your GP.

blocks.text: Why many people choose to start outside summer
blocks.html: Why many people choose to start outside summer
Many people think about skin checks after a summer holiday or when they notice a new spot.

Having Total Body Mapping before the busiest summer period has a practical advantage. It allows your GP to create a baseline before another season of beach days, fishing, gardening and time outdoors, making future comparisons more accurate.
It also gives your GP time to identify any areas they’d like to keep an eye on before your skin has another season of Queensland sun exposure.

blocks.text: When your GP recommends monitoring a spot
blocks.html: When your GP recommends monitoring a spot
Not every spot that catches your GP’s attention needs to be removed.
Sometimes, useful clinical information comes from determining whether a spot changes over time. This requires a reliable record for comparison at a future appointment.
For some patients, a GP may recommend clinical photography orTotal Body Mappingto assist with monitoring over time.

Total Body Mapping records standardised images that may help your clinician compare areas of skin at future appointments. Depending on the imaging performed, this may include areas that are difficult for you to monitor yourself.
Comparing images may provide useful clinical information. However, an unchanged appearance does not by itself exclude skin cancer.

blocks.text: When your GP recommends a skin biopsy or excision
blocks.html: When your GP recommends a skin biopsy or excision

A biopsy involves removing a sample, or sometimes the whole lesion, so it can be examined by a pathologist. Depending on the lesion and the clinical circumstances, this may involve a shave biopsy, punch biopsy or excisional biopsy. If further excision is required, your GP will explain how much additional tissue is recommended for removal and why.

A biopsy can provide information that cannot always be confirmed by examining the skin alone. The type of biopsy recommended will depend on the spot, its location and your individual clinical circumstances.
Your GP will explain the proposed procedure, its purpose, potential risks, expected benefits, alternatives and likely costs before obtaining your consent.
Skin checks at Sunstate Family Practiceare performed by GPs with experience in skin cancer assessment. Where clinically appropriate, biopsies may be performed at the practice.

blocks.text: When a spot needs to be removed
blocks.html: When a spot needs to be removed
If removal is recommended, your GP will explain what needs to be removed, why removal is recommended, what the procedure involves, the potential risks and the likely costs before proceeding.

Where clinically appropriate, skin biopsies and excisions may be performed in Sunstate Family Practice’s on-site procedure room. This allows some patients to continue this stage of their care at the same practice.
Tissue removed for diagnostic purposes is sent to pathology for examination. The pathology result helps your GP determine whether any further treatment or follow-up is required.
What if melanoma is found?

If melanoma is identified, the next steps depend on the pathology result, the clinical findings and the patient’s individual circumstances. Your GP will explain the result and discuss any further treatment, investigation, follow-up or referral that may be required.
Dr Randal Johnson discusses this question in the short video below.

blocks.text: What happens at your next skin check?
blocks.html: What happens at your next skin check?
Your GP can re-examine monitored spots, check for anything new and, where available, compare previous clinical photographs or Total Body Mapping images.

How often you should have a skin check depends on your individual risk factors and clinical circumstances. Your GP can assess your risk and advise whether regular skin checks or photographic monitoring are appropriate for you.
New or changing spots—or spots that concern you—should be assessed regardless of when you last had a skin check.

title: Skin Cancer Prevention & Screening in Queensland | Sunstate
description: Queensland has some of the world’s highest skin cancer rates. Learn how to lower your risk, when to get a skin check and how to book in Victoria Point.

blocks.html: With Queensland’s summer already packing a punch, it is a good time to learn about your skin health and when you should visit your local GP for a skin cancer screening.

Queensland is often called the “skin cancer capital of the world” as it has one of Australia’s highest prevalence of melanoma, which is also the most aggressive type of skin cancer. Over 3,600 Queenslander being diagnosed with melanoma every year!

The high prevalence of skin cancer in Queensland can be attributed to our hot climate. Queensland receives some of the highest UV radiations in the world as we are close to the equator and have many clear-blue sky days.

Therefore, it is vital that you have regular skin cancer screenings and look for any signs of cancer. Early diagnosis allows treatments to be more successful. The first line of defence for skin cancer is early detection.

blocks.text: What are the risk factors for skin cancer?
blocks.html: What are the risk factors for skin cancer?

For Brisbane, the higher UV index is one of the most common risk factors causing skin cancer. This invisible killer that neither can be seen or felt, damages your skin when overexposed to sun and is a likely leading cause of skin cancer should you fail to protect your skin.

blocks.text: There are other risks factors associated with the disease including,
blocks.html: There are other risks factors associated with the disease including,

items: Unprotected exposure to higher UV radiations
Skin that burns, freckles and reddens easily
A previous case of any skin cancer especially melanoma
A childhood history to adverse tanning and sunburn
Family medical history with skin cancer having been diagnosed with a first-degree family member
Irregular and uneven moles
Light coloured eyes, fair skin tone and red hair
Exposure to a pattern of intense UV radiations causing periods of sunburn
Older age
A weak immune system caused due to usage of immune suppression medicines

blocks.text: How to check for signs of skin cancer?
blocks.html: How to check for signs of skin cancer?

It is very important to be aware of your skin health and to know what is normal for your skin. Developing a habit of checking your skin to spot any changes is a good practice and must be regularly done. If you can recognise any changes, seek immediate help from doctors.

items: For melanoma, look for spots or changes in an existing spot such asÂ size, shape and colour.
Look for any changes in your skin, including changes to any spots, moles or rashes on your entire body. It is possible to notice skin cancer signs in areas of the body not exposed to the sun.
For nodular melanoma, check for spots that are pink or red. These spots can be uneven and raised from the skin. These spots also tend to bleed and form a crust.
To spot a basal cell cancer, the spots are dry and scaly in texture. They are more reddish and pearly in colours that grow gradually and usually appear in areas exposed to the sun.

Look for moles in your body, that change the way they appear look. Changes you should be aware of includes an increase in mole size, varying colours usually from brown to black, moles that bleed and develops a scaly and notched outline.
Look for new moles developed and itches.
A new spot or old ones that gradually raises and feels like a lump.

blocks.html: How is skin cancer diagnosed?

blocks.alt: A GP checking for skin cancer spot using a dermascope, Skin Cancer Clinic Victoria Point

blocks.html: In the majority of cases, your GP will conduct a physical examination paying attention to any signs of cancer in your skin. If deemed necessary, they will also perform a biopsy and may refer you to a skin specialist.

Physical Examination – A GP will perform a physical examination to look for signs of cancer. Questions about your current medication, medical history and lifestyle could be asked to help determine your skin condition.

Biopsy – If your doctor suspects any signs of skin cancer, part of your skin will be removed to be examined by a pathologist. This is a simple procedure which can be conducted by your doctor or a skin specialist referred by your doctor.
When should I seek help?

It is good to become familiar with the look of your skin especially with our skin moles, the blemishes, and freckles. So, if you notice any changes in their appearances such as changes in colour, shape or size, as this could be an early indicator of skin cancer.
If you notice any unusual change in your skin, you should see your doctor as early detection means greater success in treatment.

At our Victoria Point Skin Cancer Clinic, we have placed a dedicated team of GPs and allied health professionals for identifying and treating skin cancer. We use state-of-the-art technologies like artificial intelligence to provide an improved and accurate diagnosis for all our patients.
To visit our skin cancer clinic, you can avail of an online appointment or give us a call at (07) 3207 7744 for further information on our skin check services.
